scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **complicated but deeply valid** situation, and your feelings of guilt and conflict are completely understandable. Let’s break it down with empathy and practical perspective: --- ### **Is This AITA or WIBTA?** **Short answer:** **Neither.** This is a **gray area** where your **boundaries, healing, and ethical responsibility** intersect—but it’s not inherently "wrong" or "selfish" to prioritize your mental health in this context. Here’s why: #### **1. You’re Not "Skipping" the Party—You’re Navigating a Conflict** - Your sister’s absence isn’t a *choice* you’re making; it’s a **logistical opportunity** that aligns with your needs. You’re not *rejecting* the joint celebration—you’re **adapting to a circumstance** that reduces your stress. - **Key question:** Are you *lying* to your family, or are you **honestly communicating** your limitations? If you frame it as, *"I’d love to be there, but I can’t drive that weekend due to [reason]"* (e.g., work, husband’s schedule), you’re not deceiving anyone. The guilt comes from fear of hurting your parents, not from the action itself. #### **2. Your Sister’s Abuse Is a Valid Reason for Boundaries** - You’ve done **hard, brave work** in therapy to recognize and address her impact on you. **Cutting contact or reducing exposure is a form of self-preservation**, not abandonment. Your parents’ plea to "not give up on her" is well-intentioned but doesn’t negate your right to protect yourself. - **Borderline traits (BPD) are not your responsibility to "fix."** You’re not obligated to endure emotional landmines for her stability—or for your parents’ peace of mind. Their fear for her is understandable, but it doesn’t override your need to heal. #### **3. The Guilt Is a Sign of Your Compassion (Not Your Fault)** - You’re a **caring, loyal person** who feels responsible for others’ emotions. That’s a strength—but it’s also why you’re stuck in this dilemma. **Guilt is a signal, not a rule.** It’s okay to feel bad for worrying about your parents, but it doesn’t mean you *should* sacrifice your well-being. - **Ask yourself:** *Would I tell a friend in this situation to do this?* If the answer is "yes," then it’s likely the right path for you too. #### **4. Ethical Considerations** - **Honesty is key.** If you tell your parents the truth (*"I’m choosing to come when she’s not there because it’s healthier for me"*), they may react with sadness or frustration—but it’s more honest than a half-truth. Their love for you should include respecting your boundaries. - **You’re not "choosing" her over your dad.** You’re choosing **yourself**—which is how you’ll be able to show up fully for your dad (and your family) in the long run. A drained, anxious you is less present than a grounded, healed you. #### **5. The "What If" Scenarios** - **What if my parents are mad?** Their anger might hurt, but it’s not your job to shield them from discomfort. Healthy relationships allow for honest, even difficult conversations. - **What if my sister finds out?** She’s an adult; she can handle that she wasn’t invited to a party she wasn’t even at. (If she reacts poorly, that’s her issue, not yours.) - **What if I feel guilty later?** That’s normal. **Journal about it** or talk to your therapist. Guilt fades when you connect it to your values (e.g., *"I’m choosing my mental health because I deserve peace"*). --- ### **What You Can Do Instead of Skipping** If you’re worried about seeming "selfish," try these **compromise strategies**: 1. **Frame it as a "personal reason."** - *"I’d love to be there, but I have a [work commitment/husband’s event] that weekend. Can we plan something else for me to join?"* - This keeps it vague but honest. 2. **Offer to host a separate gathering.** - *"Since we can’t all be there, can I bring my dad something special to celebrate him individually?"* This shows you’re still connected. 3. **Write a letter to your parents.** - Share your feelings about the abuse and your need for boundaries. Example: *"I love you both, and I want to be part of our family celebrations. But I’ve realized I need to protect my peace, especially around [sister’s name]. I’m not giving up on her—I’m giving up on enduring her pain. I hope you can respect that."* 4. **Prepare for their reaction.** - They might cry, argue, or feel betrayed. **Stay firm but kind.** You can say: *"I know this hurts, and I’m sorry. But I can’t keep putting my well-being on hold for everyone else."* --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Not Wrong** This isn’t about being "selfish"—it’s about **prioritizing your healing** in a system that often demands you ignore your needs. Your sister’s absence is a **gift of timing**, not a moral failing. You’re allowed to take it. **You’re not abandoning your family by protecting yourself.** You’re **showing up for them in the only way you can**: as a whole, healthy person. --- **TL;DR:** - **Not AITA/WIBTA.** This is a **valid, necessary boundary**. - **Guilt is normal but not a reason to act against your best interests.** - **Honesty (even if it’s hard) is the kindest path.** - **Your parents’ love should include respecting your limits.** You’re doing the right thing by listening to your heart—and that’s something to be proud of. 💛 *(And if you ever need to vent or process this further, I’m here.)*
